1.c4 e5 2.Nc3.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Reversed Sicilian

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and takes control of d5 and e4, so White cannot build a broad centre unopposed. Black commits to no pawn structure yet and keeps every set-up open. The price is that White, with the extra tempo of a reversed Sicilian, still decides what kind of game this becomes.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Reversed Closed Sicilian
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight, guards e5 and eyes d4. Black heads for a closed game: White tends to expand on the queenside, while Black seeks counterplay with kingside pawn advances that can put White's king under pressure. It keeps the bishop and the f-pawn flexible, at the cost of a slower fight for d5.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Bb4.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Kramnik-Shirov Counterattack
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Bb4.background: Popularised by Vladimir Kramnik and Alexei Shirov, who played the opening in slightly different ways.
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Bb4.strategy: Attacks the c3-knight and threatens to take it, which would damage White's pawn structure. The bishop commits early and can be chased, so the game stays unclear and unbalanced. Black accepts a double-edged fight for the chance to unsettle White's queenside pawns.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 d6.strategy: Guards e5 with a pawn and opens the c8-bishop, aiming for a compact set-up with natural development. The pawn on d6 hems in the f8-bishop, and ...d5 now needs a second move, so White keeps more space in the centre. Sound, but passive.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Bc5.strategy: Develops the bishop towards f2 but leaves e5 without a defender, so 3.Nf3 makes Black spend the next move defending it. After 3...Nc6 the fork trick 4.Nxe5 Nxe5 5.d4 wins the piece back and leaves White with the bishop pair. Playable, but White has the easier game.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Be7.strategy: Prepares castling, but the bishop is passive on e7 and does not guard e5, which 3.Nf3 attacks at once, so Black must still spend a move defending it. Sound enough, yet White keeps the extra tempo and the easier development.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Ne7.strategy: Supports a later ...d5 and leaves c6 free for the other knight, but on e7 the knight blocks the f8-bishop and does not guard e5, which 3.Nf3 attacks at once. Sound, yet more passive than ...Nf6, and White develops freely.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7, which guards e5 and works along the long diagonal, but until the bishop arrives the h8-rook stands exposed on that diagonal. 3.d4 strikes at e5 at once, and after 3...exd4 4.Qxd4 the queen hits the rook, so Black must answer that threat at once. Playable, but less flexible than developing a knight first.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Na6.strategy: Puts a knight on the rim and aims for ...Nc5, but it does not defend e5, which 3.Nf3 attacks at once. Black must spend a further tempo while the knight is far from the action.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Qe7.strategy: Guards e5 but blocks the f8-bishop, and 3.Nd5 attacks the queen while also threatening Nxc7+. The queen has to move again to a square that guards c7, and White gains time.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Qf6.strategy: Brings the queen out early and takes f6 from the g8-knight. 3.Nd5 attacks it and threatens Nxc7+, so the queen has to move again to a square that guards c7, such as d8 or d6, and White gains time.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Qg5.strategy: Brings the queen out to a square that 3.Nf3 attacks, with e5 also hit. Black cannot save both in time: after 3...Qe7 4.Nd5 the queen is driven back again and 5.Nxe5 wins the pawn.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Qh4.strategy: Brings the queen out to a square that 3.Nf3 attacks with tempo. Black cannot hold e5 and keep time: after 3...Qf6 4.Nd5 the queen is driven back again and 5.Nxe5 wins the pawn, while 3...Qxc4 4.Nxe5 attacks the queen once more.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Bd6.strategy: Guards e5 but blocks the d-pawn, so neither ...d6 nor ...d5 is possible and the c8-bishop stays shut in. Sound, yet clumsy: the bishop has little to do on d6 and White develops freely.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nh6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it guards f7 and eyes f5 but fights for no central square. Once the d-pawn moves, Bxh6 forces gxh6 and wrecks the kingside pawns.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 a6.strategy: A waiting move that guards b5 but develops nothing. It does no harm, since ...Nc6 meets 3.Nf3, but it is a tempo spent on a rook-pawn move while White keeps the lead in development.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 a5.strategy: Takes queenside space and prevents b4, but develops nothing, and the a-pawn can no longer cover b5, a square for White's knight. 3.Nf3 attacks e5 and White gains a tempo.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 along the long diagonal, but e5 is left to be attacked by 3.Nf3 and the bishop does not defend it. The move is slow and weakens c6.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5, but takes c6 from the b8-knight and leaves e5 unguarded, so 3.Nf3 attacks it at once. Black then spends the next move on the e5-pawn instead of developing a piece.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 c5.strategy: Takes queenside space and keeps the balance, but with pawns on c5 and e5 no black pawn can ever cover d5, which becomes an outpost for a white knight. It develops nothing, so 3.Nf3 makes Black spend a move on e5. Playable, but committal.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 d5.strategy: Offers a pawn to open the centre: 3.cxd5 Nf6 4.Nf3 Nxd5 5.Nxe5 leaves White a clean pawn up, since e5 has no defender. Black gets some activity, but too little for the pawn.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 f6.strategy: Defends e5 with a pawn but takes f6 from the g8-knight, weakens e6 and the e8-h5 diagonal and develops nothing. White builds the centre at leisure and Black's king is left exposed.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 f5.strategy: Claims e4 and heads for a sharp kingside game, but weakens e6 and the e8-h5 diagonal before a piece is developed. 3.d4 hits e5 at once, and the open e-file can point at the uncastled king. Playable and double-edged, but more committal than a knight move.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 h6.strategy: A waiting move that covers g5 but develops nothing and does not guard e5. 3.Nf3 attacks e5 and gains a tempo.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 h5.strategy: Starts a kingside advance without purpose and weakens g5 and g6. It develops nothing, and 3.Nf3 attacks e5 with tempo.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Ke7.strategy: Gives up castling for good and blocks the f8-bishop and the queen's diagonal. The king is stuck in the centre where d4 can open the position, and nothing is gained for it.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Ba3.strategy: Hangs the bishop: 3.bxa3 simply wins a piece, and Black gets nothing in return.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 b5.strategy: Offers the b-pawn with no follow-up: 3.cxb5 simply wins it, and Black has no lead in development to make up for the pawn.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 g5.strategy: Loosens the kingside while e5 is undefended. 3.d4 hits e5 and opens the c1-bishop against g5, and after 3...exd4 4.Qxd4 the white queen hits the h8-rook; 4...Nf6 blocks the black queen's guard of g5, so 5.Bxg5 wins a pawn and pins the knight.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 e4.strategy: Advances the pawn to a square White attacks and Black cannot defend: 3.Nxe4 simply wins a pawn, and the extra space is gone.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 d6 3.Nf3.name: English Opening: King's English Variation
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 d6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight and tests e5 at once. Black's d6 already covers it, so there is no gain, but the knight also controls d4 and keeps every set-up open for White. A natural, flexible move that leads to a slow fight for central space.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 d6 3.g3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, so that it supports the knight's grip on d5. White picks a restrained set-up against Black's solid pawn structure and builds long-term pressure rather than striking immediately.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 d6 3.e3.strategy: A quiet set-up move: it frees the king's bishop and the queen and keeps the d-pawn ready to challenge the centre with support. It is slower than developing a knight and gives Black time to build a compact centre, so White has no more than a flexible, equal position.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 d6 3.d4.strategy: Challenges e5 at once, but the exchange brings White little: the queen recaptures on d4 and Black's knight attacks it with a gain of time. Black's pawn on d6 keeps the structure sound and without weaknesses, so White has opened the game without any lead in development.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 d6 3.g3 c6.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Keres Defence
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 d6 3.g3 c6.strategy: Covers d5 and b5, so White's pieces lose both outposts, and gives Black a compact trio of pawns on c6, d6 and e5. It is solid but slow: Black spends a move without developing a piece and leaves White the freedom to choose the plan.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 d6 3.g3 Nf6.strategy: The natural developing move: the knight takes control of e4 and d5, the squares White's fianchetto and knight aim at, and Black keeps every set-up open. Black meets the slow build-up with simple development and keeps a solid centre without committing a pawn.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 d6 3.g3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the queen's knight and adds a second guard of e5 and a say over d4, so White's central break is harder to carry out. The knight does block the c-pawn, so d5 can no longer be covered by ...c6 and a White knight may settle there, but Black keeps a solid centre.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 d6 3.g3 g6.strategy: Mirrors White's plan and prepares a bishop on the long diagonal. It is sound, a compact pawn chain with a fianchettoed bishop, but it leaves the d5 square and the centre to White, who has more space and the easier game.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 d6 3.Nf3 Bg4.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Smyslov Defence
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 d6 3.Nf3 Bg4.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain and puts pressure on the knight that covers d4. If Black takes on f3, White recaptures with a pawn and has doubled pawns, but also the two bishops and a say over how the position opens.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 d6 3.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the king's knight toward the kingside, controls e4 and d5 and prepares to castle, while the pawns on e5 and d6 stay as a solid wall. Black accepts that White has more space and aims for a sound, flexible position from which the centre can be challenged later.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 d6 3.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops with a second guard of e5 and pressure on d4, so White's central break is harder to carry out. A sound, active set-up, but the knight blocks the c-pawn and Black commits the queenside before the plan is clear.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto of the king's bishop, which adds pressure on d5 and the long diagonal while the king's knight keeps the choice between f3 and e2. White plays for a slow queenside initiative, and Black has to find counterplay on the other wing.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.Nf3.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Three Knights System
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight with an attack on e5 and keeps the pawn centre flexible. White declines the fianchetto and queenside play for classical, symmetrical development, in which White's extra tempo has to be turned into something concrete.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.e3.strategy: Opens the king's bishop and prepares Nge2 and a central break with d4, a solid set-up that keeps the fianchetto in reserve. It is slower to claim the long diagonal and d5, so Black can develop naturally and White gets less than with the fianchetto.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6.strategy: Mirrors White's plan: Black prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop and keeps a sturdy kingside, from which pawn advances can create counterplay against White's queenside expansion. The game becomes a slow, symmetrical manoeuvring battle.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 d6.strategy: Supports e5 with a pawn and opens the c8-bishop, a compact set-up that does not contest d5 or the long diagonal. It is sound but passive: White completes the fianchetto and builds queenside play at leisure while Black must find counterplay elsewhere.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 f5.strategy: Grabs space on the kingside: the pawns on e5 and f5 restrain White's centre and give Black real counterplay against the queenside plan. The price is a looser king and a weak e6 square, and the pawns must not run ahead without support.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the king's knight toward castling and watches e4 and d5, so White's fianchetto meets natural development. Black keeps the structure flexible, but has no plan of its own yet: the slow queenside expansion goes unchallenged for the moment.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 d6 4.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop eyes the c6 knight and, with the c4 pawn and the c3 knight, controls d5, so Black cannot challenge the centre with ...d5. White keeps every plan open, and the queenside advance can start whenever it likes.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 d6 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight toward quick castling and adds pressure on e5, with the fianchetto still to come. A natural, flexible move that sets Black no problems; White's extra tempo decides nothing yet and the plan has to be chosen later.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 d6 4.d3.strategy: Supports c4 and e4 and opens the c1-bishop, a modest move that builds a compact pawn centre. It spends a tempo on a pawn and leaves d4 without a white pawn guarding it, so a black knight can jump there at once.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 d6 4.Bg2 Be6.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Troger Defence
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 d6 4.Bg2 Be6.strategy: Develops the bishop with a threat against the undefended c4 pawn, so White must react at once. A natural way to gain a tempo, though the bishop can be challenged on e6 and the pawn is easily defended.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 d6 4.Bg2 Nf6.strategy: The natural developing move: the knight covers e4 and d5 and prepares castling, so the fianchetto is met with harmonious development. With e5 already guarded by the d-pawn, Black has a sound centre and can decide the rest of the set-up later.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 d6 4.Bg2 g6.strategy: Mirrors White with the fianchetto of the king's bishop. With the d-pawn already guarding e5, Black gets a compact set-up and quick castling; the bishop is hemmed in by its own e5 pawn for now, and the game stays a slow manoeuvring one.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2.strategy: Develops the king's bishop on the long diagonal, controlling d5 and eyeing the c6 knight. White completes the fianchetto while the king's knight can still choose its square and the queenside advance can begin whenever White likes.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Rb1.strategy: Prepares the queenside pawn advance at once, with the rook on the b-file as its base. It is slow: the bishop and the king's knight stay undeveloped, and Black has time to organise counterplay on the kingside.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight with pressure on e5 and keeps the choice between a central break and the fianchetto open. A natural, flexible move: the game can stay slow and symmetrical or open in the centre, depending on how White continues.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Taimanov Variation
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7.strategy: Completes the mirror-image fianchetto. The bishop is blocked by its own e5 pawn for now, but it guards the kingside dark squares and is ready for the day the centre opens. Black accepts a solid, symmetrical game and must find a pawn lever for counterplay.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 d6.strategy: Supports e5 with a pawn and frees the c8-bishop, so Black secures the centre first and finishes the kingside set-up afterwards. A solid, flexible order, though the king's bishop still has to reach g7 before Black castles.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight toward castling and covers e4 and d5, so White's long-diagonal bishop meets natural development. Black keeps the fianchetto of the king's bishop in reserve and heads for a solid, symmetrical game.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.d3.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Closed System
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.d3.strategy: Supports the c4 pawn and keeps the centre solid, leaving White free to push in the centre later or to expand on the queenside. A slow, flexible build-up in which neither side has committed, and the game is decided in the middlegame.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.e3.strategy: Prepares to strike in the centre with d4 and to develop the king's knight on e2, so that the long diagonal stays open. White plays for a central break that opens lines for the queenside attack, at the price of a temporarily shut-in c1-bishop.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.Rb.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Hungarian Attack
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.Rb.strategy: Prepares the queenside pawn advance without delay, with the rook behind the b-pawn. It does nothing for the centre or the king's knight, so Black has time to build a solid centre and play on the other wing.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.d3.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Closed System, Full Symmetry
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.d3.strategy: Backs up e5 with a pawn and mirrors White exactly, leaving the c8-bishop free to develop. Black keeps the centre closed and solid and waits to see how White commits, since neither side has a weakness to attack yet.
Develops the king's knight, covers e4 and d5 and prepares castling, without yet committing the d-pawn. The game stays symmetrical and slow, and Black develops as easily as White does.

A compact development of the knight that keeps the f-pawn free to advance. The knight is less active than on f6, since it does not watch e4, and it gives Black little with which to challenge White's build-up.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.d3.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Botvinnik System
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.d3.background: Classified as an English although White can play it against a variety of Black defences, with c4, Nc3, d3, e4, g3, Bg2 and Ne2 in some order. Its pawn structure appears in one of Botvinnik's treatments of the English.
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.d3.strategy: Takes space and tightens White's grip on d5, steering the game into a closed manoeuvring battle. The price is the d4 square: no white pawn guards it any more, so a black knight can settle there and White has to watch for it.

Develops the king's knight and prepares castling while the e-pawn stays at home, so the centre remains flexible. A natural, risk-free development after which White chooses between a central advance and queenside play.
Prepares the queenside pawn advance at once, with the rook already on the b-file. It is slow: the king's knight stays at home and Black has time to develop and organise counterplay on the other wing.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.e3.strategy: Backs up e5 and frees the c8-bishop. Black answers White's slow build-up with a solid centre and keeps the kingside pawn advance for later, a sound reply that leaves White to commit first.

Develops the king's knight toward castling and covers e4 and d5. Black answers White's slow build-up with straightforward development and keeps the pawn centre flexible, leaving White to show where the play will be.
A compact development of the knight that keeps the f-pawn free to advance. The knight is less active than on f6, since it does not watch e4, and Black does little to hinder White's central plans.
Develops the knight to e2 instead of f3, which keeps the g2-bishop's diagonal open and avoids a pin by ...Bg4. It also supports a later central break with d4, the thematic idea behind e3.

Develops the king's knight toward castling and adds pressure on e5. Black can pin it with ...Bg4, a nuisance more than a problem, since White can break the pin with h3 or accept the exchange of bishop for knight.
Prepares the queenside pawn advance at once, with the rook already on the b-file. It is slow: both knights are still at home and Black has time to develop and organise counterplay on the kingside.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.e3.name: English Opening: Closed, Taimanov Variation
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.e3.strategy: Puts the knight where it backs a ...f5 advance, counterplay on the kingside against White's queenside plans. The knight on the rim is safe for now: White's e3 has shut the c1-bishop in, so there is no Bxh6 to double the pawns.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.e3.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Bremen-Hort Variation
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.e3.strategy: Develops the bishop with a real threat to win the undefended c4 pawn, so White must defend or challenge it at once. Black gains a tempo and keeps the f-pawn and the knight flexible, but the bishop on e6 can be traded off or harassed.

The natural reply: the knight covers e4 and d5 and Black is ready to castle, with a sound centre and a compact set-up. Black develops the last minor piece to its best square and waits to see whether White plays on the queenside or in the centre.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Rb1 Nh6.strategy: Prepares ...f5 and kingside counterplay at once: the knight supports the f5 advance and can come to f7. Black answers White's slow queenside plan with play on the other wing before White has developed the bishop.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Rb1 Bg7.strategy: Completes the mirror-image fianchetto at once, so Black is set while White's rook still waits on b1 for the queenside advance. The bishop is blocked by its own e5 pawn for now, but it guards the dark squares and prepares castling.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Rb1 d6.strategy: Supports e5 with a pawn and frees the c8-bishop, a solid way to meet the slow rook move. Black keeps the centre closed and has time to complete the set-up, because White's queenside plan takes a while to bite.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Rb1 Nh6 5.Bg.strategy: Completes the fianchetto, so the rook move now looks like useful preparation for the queenside advance and not a loss of time. The bishop controls d5 and eyes the c6 knight, and White's set-up is complete.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Rb1 Nh6 5.Nf.strategy: Develops the king's knight with pressure on e5 and keeps the fianchetto for the next move. The knight on the rim helps little in the centre, so White can finish development calmly before the queenside plan starts.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Rb1 Nh6 5.d3.strategy: Supports c4 and e4 and opens the c1-bishop, which now eyes the knight on h6. A modest move: a trade on h6 is easily met by recapturing with the bishop, and the fianchetto is still to be played.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Rb1 Nh6 5.Bg.name: English Opening: Closed, Taimanov Variation
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Rb1 Nh6 5.Bg.strategy: Completes the fianchetto and mirrors White. With the knight on h6 ready to support ...f5, Black has a plan of kingside counterplay against the queenside advance, in a solid, symmetrical set-up.

Plays the move the knight was posted for: the pawns on e5 and f5 take space and restrain White's centre, and kingside counterplay begins at once. The price is a looser king and a weak e6 square, and the pawns need support.

Supports e5 with a pawn and frees the c8-bishop, a solid choice that keeps the knight on h6 ready for a later pawn advance on the kingside. It costs a tempo on defence, but White's queenside plan is slow.
